new_statements.quote: Como en la variedad sureña del aimara (Briggs, 1993: 25), el acento del aimara moqueguano es, primordialmente, grave, es decir, aparece en la penúltima sílaba. En este sentido, Cerrón-Palomino (2000: 177) afirma que es predecible y Martín (2001: 43), que no es fonémico. La variedad presenta reacomodación de acento al introducirse nuevos elementos en la palabra. Como se desprende, entonces, el acento en el aimara no cumple ningún valor distintivo. [...] uta [u.ta] 'casa' / utanaka [u.ta.na.ka] 'casas' [...] (p.121:) el acento de intensidad aparece en la penúltima sílaba.
new_statements.translation: As in the southern variety of Aymara (Briggs 1993: 25), stress in Moquegua Aymara is primarily paroxytone, i.e. it falls on the penultimate syllable. In this respect Cerrón-Palomino (2000: 177) states that it is predictable and Martín (2001: 43) that it is not phonemic. The variety shows re-placement of stress when new elements are added to the word. It follows, then, that stress in Aymara has no distinctive value. [...] uta 'house' / utanaka 'houses' [...] (p.121:) intensity stress appears on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the (fully suffixed) word and shifts rightward as suffixes are added; it is predictable and non-contrastive. Chilean-Aymara descriptions (Salas & Valencia 1988: 120; Poblete & Salas 1997: 149-150) say the same: fixed penultimate stress realised as slightly greater length/intensity/pitch, demarcative not contrastive, with coda glides not counting as vowels.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned by Cépeda Cáceres; Salas & Valencia and Poblete & Salas say all non-penultimate syllables are roughly equal (final syllable lower and laxer), i.e. no secondary stress described.
new_statements.exceptions: Cépeda Cáceres says 'primordialmente' (primarily) penultimate without listing exceptions. Salas & Valencia 1988: 121 note an exceptional oxytone [aká] (demonstrative) in connected speech with stress displacement on the following noun; Cerrón-Palomino & Carvajal 2009 (pan-Aymara) note surface oxytones from long vowels attracting stress and from final-vowel elision after penultimate assignment.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (examples are isolated words with suffixes: uta -> utanaka, juma -> jumampi); Poblete & Salas explicitly state the rule for 'la palabra aymara aislada' and use the 3-1 contour to delimit the simple word; phrase-final vowel elision can yield surface final stress in connected speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Primary quote is from Cépeda Cáceres 2011, describing the Aymara of Moquegua (districts around Carumas/San Cristóbal, southern Peru) = Southern Aymara [ayc] sout2996 proper (same region as Coler's Muylaq' Aymara, Muylaque, Moquegua). Corroborating statements (Salas & Valencia 1988, Isluga/Iquique; Poblete & Salas 1997, Aymara of Chile) describe Chilean altiplano Aymara, which Glottolog's bibliography files under sout2996 but Ethnologue counts under Central Aymara [ayr]; all three agree on fixed penultimate stress, as does the pan-Aymara description (Cerrón-Palomino & Carvajal 2009) already held under cent2142.

sources.note: Sec. 2.1.4 'Régimen acentual': Aymara (Bolivia, pan-dialectal) carries intensity stress on the penultimate syllable, fixed and automatic under suffixation; apparent oxytones arise from vowel lengthening attracting stress or from final-vowel suppression after normal penultimate assignment. General Aymara, not specific to the southern variety.

sources.note: Sec. 1.1.13 'Rasgos suprasegmentales' pp.149-150: penultimate syllable slightly longer, higher and more intense, last syllable shorter/lower/lax; 'acento de longitud, intensidad y altura fijo en la penúltima sílaba.. el acento no cumple función contrastiva, sino más bien demarcativa' (word = syllable string delimited by the 3-1 contour); in the isolated word stress always falls on the penultimate vowel, glides [j, w] in coda do not count.
